I am convinced they will not have the same opportunity in life they would have had if their fathers had returned. We have discussed

this matter in veterans affairs committees on different occasions. The veterans organizations across the country are in favour of some such step being taken. I do not believe there is anybody in the house who would not approve of grants of that kind being made. I hope the department will give consideration to setting up some system whereby that kind of grant can be made available to the children of the men who did not come back.
I should like also to say a word or two about war veterans allowance. As the minister knows, the war veterans allowance was set up to provide for the front line soldier who was burnt out because he had been under Are. He could not establish that his disability was directly attributable to his service, and therefore he could not qualify for a pension, but it was felt that because of his service he was entitled to aid from the state. He was given the war veterans allowance, which is commonly referred to as the burnt-out pension. There was a certain honour and dignity about having that allowance. The veteran who got it felt that he was not getting relief. He felt he was getting something for his service. It was really remuneration for services rendered. All of us would like to keep it on that basis. Therefore I believe it is a great mistake for the department only to provide for additional benefits, over and above the statutory war veterans allowance, on the basis of the man showing that he has not any assets and that he cannot get along. In other words, it is being administered as a type of relief.
Let me give the minister an example. An old friend of mine was unable to get by. He was living in the interior of British Columbia. I made application on his behalf for an increase in the allowance. He had no other income and I thought he would be given either the full $10 a month or whatever amount it was decided should be paid. An investigator went up to look into his case. The chief difficulty of this applicant was that he was unable to afford clothing. The grant given to him was not a money grant; he was given so much to buy clothes. The war veterans allowance is being administered as a relief measure in the same way that relief was administered to small pensioners during the depression days. In my opinion it takes away from the recipient of war veterans allowance the feeling that he is getting something as a right, and because he had been a front-line soldier. He is put in the same category as if he had gone to the city and asked for relief. I do not think it is sound.
May I urge upon the minister that an amendment be introduced to increase the war veterans allowance from $40.41 to $50 for a single man, and at least to $85 for a married

man. A married recipient may receive only $70.83 now. I believe that is the maximum amount per month. He was getting $60 before and it was raised to a maximum of $70.83, just as the amount for a single man has been raised $10. I think that a married man should be allowed more than $70.83. The Legion has suggested $85. The present payment is not on a satisfactory basis.
Another unsatisfactory feature is that the increase is based on a yearly parliamentary grant. It is not written into the statute. A grant may be brought down and voted this year, and next year a grant may not be brought down. The increase should be written into the statute. In British Columbia the old age pensioners are now getting more than most of the war veterans allowance recipients. The veterans are being put in an inferior position. I have here a clipping from a publication issued by the department, the name of which I forget.
"Veterans Affairs".

The issue I have is dated July L, 1949, and I point out to the minister that in it he is quoted as having said at Fort William:
I made It quite clear at the Saskatoon convention that I felt that the government must keep some general relationship between war veterans allowance and old age pensions. I still maintain that stand.
Those are the minister's own words.

I know that the hon. member wants to be fair. I do not know whether or not the rest of my remarks were quoted there, but whether or not they are I did go on to say that there were certain factors affecting war veterans allowance which did not apply to old age pensions in any province, namely, the payment of the allowance ten years earlier, the fact that it carried with it medical care and attention, and also the fact that a man could have his wife drawing the wife's allowance at age twenty-five, if he was married in time. Those are real factors on the credit side.
Of course the difference in age is to compensate the veteran for his service.
Burnt out.

In reality it is the veteran's old age pension. As to hospitalization, old age pensioners in British Columbia receive hospitalization free of charge. They get just as much hospitalization as a veteran. That may not be true in all provinces but it is so in British Columbia. I suggest that the veteran should at least be on the same basis as the old age pensioner, and in the provinces of British Columbia and Alberta he is in an inferior position at the present time.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
And Saskatchewan.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South says that is also true of Saskatchewan. I was not trying to overlook Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: We will take that qualification on division.

So much for the amount of the war veterans allowance. I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Yorkton speak as he did today about the question of paying war veterans allowance to imperial veterans. The Legion has requested that for many years, and the merits of the request are good. These men came to Canada shortly after the first great war. They gave up their rights to social security in Great Britain which were greater than they could get in Canada. They threw in their lot with us. In the recent war many of them served with our veterans guard. Their sons served with our sons. Nevertheless even the men who served in the veterans guard cannot qualify for the war veterans allowance unless they went out of Canada, and very few were able to do that.
I think it is generally admitted that they are Canadians and should be treated as such. No one has been asking that they be paid pensions. We are asking that they have the right to the war veterans allowance. Some of them served at Mons in 1914, and today their position is tragic. We have many of these men in British Columbia. If they become destitute they have to go on city relief. Before the election they were all told that a survey was being made of the whole question of the war veterans allowance for imperials, and I think we should be told at this session whether or not they will get that allowance.
Then finally I want to say a word about the Canadians who served in the merchant navy. To the man in the street, and indeed to everyone in this house, they were the fourth arm of the service; they lost a larger proportion of their numbers than any of the other three fighting services. During the war they were treated as one of the fighting services. I have before me the speech from the throne delivered on September 6, 1945. Of course we know this speech is drawn up by the Prime Minister, or at all events by the government; and it contains these words:
Our country will ever remember with pride the heroic exploits of Canada's fighting men and merchant seamen.
I have in my files a dozen quotations from various ministers of the crown to the effect that the merchant seamen were the fourth arm of the service, and they should have been treated as belonging to the fighting services.

Supply-Veterans Affairs I believe the Minister of Veterans Affairs is of that opinion, together with his department. I do not blame the Department of Veterans Affairs for not having given these men the proper treatment, but I do blame the Department of Transport. Throughout the whole affair that department has adopted a heartless, merciless attitude toward these men who served in Canada's merchant navy, and I hope that during this session that situation will be remedied.
Many of these men have lost their health. I have in my hand a letter from a young lad who served in the Canadian merchant navy for five years, four of them during the war. Even now I think he is only twenty-two or twenty-three years old. He is lying in the provincial tuberculosis hospital at Jericho Beach, Vancouver, very ill with tuberculosis. He developed malaria and pneumonia in 1945 on a trip from the west coast of Africa to Philadelphia, where he was taken off the ship and placed in hospital. When he had recovered sufficiently to travel, he was sent back to Vancouver. There he was examined by the doctor of the manning pool, who insisted that he have an X-ray. That was done; and it now develops that when the X-ray was sent back it was accompanied by a report to the effect that he should have six months' rest. Instead of that, through some carelessness on the part of the medical men in Vancouver, that lad was sent back to sea. A little later it was found that he had a very serious case of tuberculosis, which dated back to his first illness. There is no justification for the government refusing to accept responsibility for this man. The last paragraph of the letter he wrote me reads:
You cannot deny that the merchant navy did its share during the war. Why then the discrimination? In the same ward with me are two exservice men who during the course of the war never left the province of British Columbia, yet are drawing a one hundred per cent pension, while I am being paid for my service at the rate of $3 a month. Does this seem fair to you?
Even that $3 per month is paid by the province. There is no justice here. The law should be amended to provide that these men are entitled to pension. In addition, they can get no educational benefits; they are not permitted to go to university. Until this spring they could only get vocational training if they intended to go back to sea; and Canada's merchant navy has been so reduced that there have been practically no openings for young men who want to follow the sea as a career. Yet they were unable to obtain training for anything else. Last December I believe an order in council was passed providing that they could obtain vocational training if they applied by the end of June and if they were

under thirty years of age. That was a recommendation of the last veterans affairs committee, which in my view was an improper recommendation, I do not think the committee gave its usual thorough consideration to this question. To back up my statement may I tell the minister that I believe less than one-tenth of the men who have applied for that vocational training since the order in council passed last December have been able to qualify. The figures given to me in August showed that only 47 out of 518 applicants had been accepted for vocational training. I believe too that they cannot qualify unless they served on Canadian ships, although in some cases they were sent by the Canadian manning pools to serve on allied ships. Here again there is no justification for the treatment being meted out to these merchant navy lads.
Further they get no hospitalization unless they are pensioners, and very few have been able to qualify for pensions. They do not get the civil service preference. They are not entitled to business and professional loans. They cannot take up land or a small holding under the Veterans Land Act unless they are pensioners; and they are not permitted to get a house even in these subdivisions being built up by the government for veterans. They are not classed as veterans for that purpose.
I can only bring this matter to the attention of the house, but I suggest that this treatment being given the men of the merchant navy is sufficient reason for setting up a committee of this house. That question can only be gone into thoroughly in such a committee; and I do hope the minister will see to it not only that these different things are dealt with but also that a committee is set up at the present session.

The points I have to make this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, have been very well covered by the hon. members who have spoken already, including the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, the hon. member for Kamloops, the hon. member for Nanaimo, the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Kootenay West. However, there are certain matters one can always find to bring to the attention of the department that have been overlooked by others. For that reason, I should like to advocate the setting up of a committee on veterans affairs and adding to the scope of that committee matters dealing with the merchant navy. In common with the last speaker, I am firmly convinced that the merchant navy has been shabbily treated and some attention should be given to it by a committee.

The main subject in my brief speech is the British veteran who resides in this country. I realize that the problem of this veteran has not been dealt with to the satisfaction of the Canadian Legion. It is the feeling of the government that the British veteran is a newcomer to this country, even though he may have resided here twenty or thirty years. He is not regarded as a Canadian entitled to qualify for these benefits. Many of these veterans who served during the first war are now anywhere from fifty to seventy years of age and, naturally, pensionable cases. Most of them have to rely on the pension for their livelihood. I can assure hon. members of this house that the British pension when translated into Canadian funds was never sufficient to give a high standard of living, but now that devaluation has taken place that pension is totally inadequate. Many of these veterans have had to go on relief. I consider it undignified to pay a veteran who gave his services to his country some form of relief in addition to his pension. I cannot understand why the government, instead of giving him relief and a pension, cannot, by combining the two payments in one pension cheque, remove the indignity of forcing him to accept relief.
Formerly the imperial veterans cashed their pension cheques at a preferred rate. I cannot see why that procedure cannot be followed today. It may cost Canada a little money, but not a great deal, and that extra money would be spent in Canada anyway. At the same time, I should like to advocate the abolition of the means test. This subject has been well covered, but I do assure the minister it is a sore point with the veterans right across this country. Many of them have requested that I bring it to the attention of the house. I would say such a test is a violation of the trust we placed in those veterans. When they went overseas we promised them the very best and upon their return they find these pinpricks to annoy them.
These are a few of the reasons why this committee on veterans affairs should be set up. Many excellent suggestions have been made this afternoon and the logical and concise way of dealing with them would be through a committee which could recommend action on them. I realize there are possibly only two or three hundred veterans affected, but I should like to mention the student veterans in the United States. These veterans have also suffered from the devaluation of the Canadian dollar. A student receives approximately $60 per month which, after the ten per cent devaluation, nets him about $54. With the high cost of living in the 45781-40i
Supply-Veterans Affairs United States, it is impossible for the veteran student to make ends meet.
Many of these students return to their home during the summer and earn a little money to assist them during the university term. It is generally conceded that the cost of living in the United States is much higher than in Canada. I would suggest to the minister that the veterans who are attending university in the United States be paid in United States currency or that the department make up the loss through devaluation. I say that, because the veterans who entered those universities were given the blessing of the department. I am satisfied that the government did the proper thing in giving these boys such an excellent opportunity. I know some students receive assistance from their parents, but some care should be taken to provide for those whose parents are not in a position to assist them. No student should be forced, because of financial need, to give up a course before he has completed it.
Two or three years ago the university of British Columbia had over four hundred medical students. When those students sought to continue their courses in Canada the veterans affairs committee did its utmost to place them, but found it impossible to place all of them. If I remember correctly, less than ten per cent were placed in Canada. Some went to China, some to South Africa and many to the United States. It is presumed that most of those students had high qualifications and will complete their course. Those boys having received the blessing of the Department of Veterans Affairs, I would plead with that department to see that they are given the opportunity of completing their course. It would not cost a great deal, since there are only two hundred involved.
One other matter I should like to mention concerns admittance to hospital. I am wondering whether the procedure could be simplified through the cutting of red tape. The veterans from the interior of British Columbia, for instance, who have reason to go to a hospital, have to go to Shaughnessy, and I was wondering whether arrangements could not be made to examine them locally. This would obviate the necessity of making the long, arduous journey to Vancouver merely for an examination. I would suggest to the department that this type of examination could very well be carried out at a local point near the veterans' homes.
In closing, I would urge the department to seriously reconsider its decision regarding the setting up of a veterans affairs committee and the giving of that committee the subject of merchant navy veterans for consideration as well.

Supply-Veterans Affairs

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Before the minister speaks, Mr. Chairman, may I say a few words on one point. I shall not take the time to repeat the representations that have been made by other members because my support of a number of the points they have been urging is already on record. I felt it might not be amiss, however, for at, least one non-veteran to participate in this discussion so that it would be clear that the rest of us are with the veterans in their concern for the best possible deal for their comrades.
I could illustrate the one point I have in mind by telling of an experience of mine a few months ago. I was asked by some friends to visit an old couple living on the third floor of a house in Winnipeg. It was not in my constituency, nor was it in the constituency of my hon. friend, the parliamentary assistant to the minister (Mr. Mutch); so that narrows it down quite a bit. Both these old people were in their seventies. The person who requested me to make the visit said it was felt the old couple should be receiving the old age pension. However, they had a great deal of pride and did not want to apply for the pension. In addition to that, the couple owned a few government bonds and they were under the impression they would have to sign them over to the government. For that reason they did not want to apply for the old age pension.
I came into the picture, as I say, because my friends thought possibly I would be able to persuade them that the old age pension arrangements were not quite as bad as they thought. I made the visit and made it known to the couple that my interest was simply that of trying to help them. During the first half hour that I spent with them I was met with an icy stare and refusal to apply for old age pensions. I was not going to give up as surrounding conditions made it obvious those people should have the pension. In due course, the old gentleman started talking about things in the past. He brought out a picture of himself taken many years ago in which he was wearing a uniform. That immediately brought to my mind the possibility that he would be able to qualify for war veterans allowance. I made that suggestion to him and you would have been amazed if you could have seen the different reaction I got from this old gentleman. He had not even known that there was something which, by virtue of his services as a veteran, he might be entitled to. That was a different story. His face brightened up and his whole conversation became much more free than it had been while I was trying to persuade him to apply for the old age pension. He began to discuss some details. That day he did not tell me, although he did

later on, how much money he had in bonds. But at any rate, he was willing for me to turn his name in to the D.V.A. people down in the Commercial building in Winnipeg and for them to come to see him in order to ascertain if something could be done. As I say, if I had known at the time how much money he had, I would have known that this suggestion was not going to work. But I had to wait to find it out. When the D.V.A. people came from the Commercial building to see him and looked into his case, they found that he had too much in the way of liquid assets; and he was told that he would have to wait until he had dissipated-perhaps they did not use that word-or spent his liquid assets and they had got down to the point of about $1,700 or $1,800 before he could qualify for the war veterans allowance. This old gentleman made this known to me in a letter. I was disappointed, but I went to see him again. It so happened, to bring the story to a speedy conclusion, that making that application at least did the trick. They got into the frame of mind in which they were prepared to try and get something of what was coming to them, and I was then able to persuade them to put in their application for the old age pension. I pointed out to them that the old age pension authorities- and some of us think they are mean enough- would treat their liquid assets in a different manner. The old age pension authorities do not say: You must wait until your liquid assets are reduced to a certain amount. They say: We will give you a pension now, reduced by the computed value of the liquid assets that you have. It was only a matter of a few months until this old couple, who had been living on an amount so small that I do not know how they got by, received an old age pension making up the difference between the computed value of their liquid assets and the ceiling of $90 per month.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That is, the computed annuity value.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That is right; the difference between the computed annuity value of the amount they had in Canadian government bonds and the $90 ceiling. The amount of old age pension which this old couple were able to get was in excess of the total of what they had been living on for I do not know how long. That particular story came out quite nicely. But the reason I am telling it and the point I am trying to impress on the minister is that-and it is in line with arguments that have been made here before- in many respects the burnt-out pension is inferior to the old age pension. That is one point as to which it seems to me a change ought to be made. I go the whole way with

the suggestions that have been made by other members. But it is soon discovered around here, and the hon. member for Yorkton will discover it too, that you must get these things by pressing for them step by step. Surely that is one step that could be taken, namely, that a change could be made in the means test provision with respect to the burnt-out pension so that the liquid assets that a veteran holds will be treated in the same way as they are treated in the case of the old age pension. I hope that change at least might be made.

As all the members of the committee seem to be laying their grievances on the doorstep of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, and as a great many of them have to do with the war veterans allowance, I might as well put mine on the minister's doorstep also. The case that I wish to bring to his attention seems to be a particularly hard one. It is that of an old couple. The wife of the pensioner is now sixty-eight years of age. Her husband was in receipt of the war veterans allowance for I do not know how long back. In 1942 or 1943, when there was a great demand for workers, she took a position in a laundry as a seamstress. Evidently they did not report her earnings to the war veterans allowance board until the authorities found it out some three, four or five years afterwards. In any case, when they did find it out, because of the earnings of the wife there had been an overpayment to this man from the war veterans allowance board of something over $2,600. The board then notified them that they would discontinue his war veterans allowance until the amount would be paid. He was also getting a small disability pension, and they were wanting him to sign that over as well.
Not being a veteran, I admit that I do not know as much about the regulations and the legislation on the matter as do some of the other members on all sides of the house who can speak from experience. But I did know that they could not touch his disability benefit and I told him not to sign it over. I think that was about a year ago. Shortly before I came down here for this session, this man's wife got in touch with me again, saying that they were at their wits' end. The disability pension was $31.25. She had stopped working in the laundry, and that has been their total income for several months, or perhaps a year or more. She appealed to the municipality for assistance and received it for a couple of months. She had to tell her story and they got in touch with the D.V.A. in Vancouver, with the result that the municipal assistance stopped as well. I wrote to the chairman of the war veterans allowance board under date of July 23, and
Supply-Veterans Affairs I am just going to quote a brief paragraph from the letter I received in reply. He referred to the man's file and said:
On perusing same I find that a large overpayment has accumulated over a period of years due to concealment of income and wilful misrepresentations on his part.
The matter of recovery of this debt due to the crown was placed in the hands of the Department of Justice a few months ago, and until the matter is cleared up from this angle the board can take no further action towards the reinstatement of the allowance.
If I have figured it out right, the date when they stopped the allowance was February, 1947. If this man had committed a crime, surely they should have taken criminal action against him long ago; because I imagine it is a matter for criminal action, unless it is one for an action for small debt. I do not know just which it is. I am not at all condoning the concealment of the income that was made, although I think that when a woman at the age of sixty-two or sixty-three goes out to earn a little money, she is entitled to it. As a matter of fact, she told me how it was spent. It was spent in paying accumulated grocery debts, in shingling the roof of what she said was the shack in which they were living, in getting dental work done and various other things.
I suggested to the war veterans allowance board that since it was impossible for these people to live on $31.25 a month they should certainly give them a war veterans allowance in order to enable them to live, because it is quite apparent that they will not get any municipal assistance. This is a deplorable situation, and from what I have heard today it is quite apparent that it is not the only one. I suggest that these people be treated more humanely and that at least their economic situation at the moment be taken into consideration. If this man is taken to court, if the Department of Justice gives that advice, if he is sent to jail, and if he has no other way to pay-they cannot fine him because he cannot pay-he will be looked after in jail and perhaps his wife can get along better on his disability pension. I assume that that would be paid in any case. Surely that is not a civilized way to deal with these cases. I would plead with the Minister of Veterans Affairs to see that he try to deal with these cases more in the line of civilized human behaviour.

What measures, if any, is the department taking to make up to imperial war veterans the losses which they are sustaining in their income from Britain because of the reduction in the value of the pound? I have a representation on that matter. It is. a serious matter.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
May I ask the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) to bring to my attention the case which he has cited?
I shall do that.

In reply to the question which has just been asked, may I say that my department is taking no steps with regard to that matter except this. Quite naturally, since the British ministry of pensions have a very active office in Ottawa, I have spoken to the head of that office regarding that matter, and he has spoken to me about it. I know very well that he has, as I have, received representations from pensioners from the United Kingdom in all parts of Canada. He has told me, and he said that I was at liberty to use it, that he has brought these representations to the attention of the ministry in London. Beyond that we have done nothing in the matter.

Does not the minister think that something ought to be done for these people? We know the position that Britain is in. It looks to me as if we are to have in a small way something like that which the hon. member for Vancouver East has pointed out. We shall have people actually suffering in Canada because of events over which they have not even the slightest control.

I fully realize the difficulty. There is of course the very distinct priority of responsibility in these matters. One of the speakers this afternoon pointed out the difficulty that Canadian students were experiencing in the United States owing to the adjustment of exchange rates as between Canada and the United States. But there again that is not the whole problem with regard to our own veterans. Approximately there are two hundred such students, but side by side with them there are about 7,000 Canadian disability pensioners of both wars resident in the United States. The same situation applies to them as applies to the smaller number of students. One could go on and quote many direct and indirect effects of this adjustment of currency but I do not feel that we have any greater responsibility in making adjustment with those from the United Kingdom who are pensioners in Canada than the United States has in making an adjustment for our pensioners who are resident in the United States. I wish it were otherwise. That is all I can say on it at the present time.
I am sure that hon. gentlemen who have spoken this afternoon would not expect me to attempt to cover all the points raised. I bespeak a chance for either my parliamentary
IMr. Blackmore.]
assistant or myself to go into full details which we shall try to do before the estimates are passed. We shall try to deal with all the questions brought up.
With the exception of two or three speakers, all who have spoken this afternoon have made strong representations on behalf of either a standing committee or a special committee on veterans affairs. I should like to say a word about that. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra pointed out, between 1943 and 1946, before I came into the house, the house had to consider some 21 pieces of new legislation for the benefit of new veterans from 1939 to 1945. It is only natural that there should be a great deal of intensified work done on that legislation in drafting it, in calling witnesses from all parts of Canada from many organizations, and in working it out. Frankly, as I look at it, and I never had any part in it, I say it must have been a tremendous task. But as I see it, and as I read the records, it appears to me that it was dealing almost entirely with new legislation.
In 1948 the government brought forward some amendments to two of these bills which had become law, namely, the Pension Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act. As well there were some other acts for minor amendments. A special committee was set up for the purpose of considering that legislation. That committee sat and, from my observation, it is worthy of all the good words that have been said about it this afternoon. It did an excellent job, and as one hon. member so well put it this afternoon, as far as was humanly possible, it was free of partisan politics. They presented their report. I cannot agree with one speaker who said today that not many of these recommendations had been accepted, because most of them were; nevertheless the factors entering into the report had to do mainly with the legislation that had been brought before it. It is true that it did discuss such matters as a further increase in war veterans allowances, the merchant marine and many others, but what I am coming to is this. We should clarify our thoughts as to whether a parliamentary committee, whether a special committee or some other, should be called upon to check on other matters in addition to legislation or amendments to come before the house. I am not going to express an opinion on that at this particular time. All that I am going to say is that there are a number of committees suggested to the government now. There is a resolution on the order paper suggesting the setting up of a committee on social security, housing and health and welfare. It is proposed that there should be a committee

on national defence, on atomic control and on many other questions.
I know that the matter of committees in general, as it was put by the hon. member for Kamloops, should receive careful study, so as to get the greatest value from these committees. I think I can assure this committee that the government will give that study. I do not propose at this particular time, to recommend to my colleagues that a committee be set up at this fall session. Beyond that I am not prepared to go, with regard to committees.
May I, though, between now and six o'clock, touch at random upon one or two points which have been brought out. Two hon. members who spoke referred to the old soldier settlement board, and the remaining amounts owing to the board by veterans who have held lands these many years. I know well the arguments made in later years on behalf of those settlers-and strong arguments they are, there can be no question.
I believe however, as I indicated at the final meeting of the committee a year ago, that it boils down to this. Members who knew some of those settlers will remember that there were many of them who conscientiously made their payments of principal and interest just as regularly as it was possible for them to do. If they did not do it, it was because they could not do it. Most of them, long before this year of 1949, have fulfilled their contracts and obtained title by grinding through, paying their debts and getting their work done. I believe it is also true to say that there are a number who, through those years, perhaps could have made their annual payments, but did not do so. Representatives of the board allowed those to run on, and at the present time they are shown as outstanding accounts.
Putting it on that simple basis, I am wondering whether or not if last year or the year before we had said, or this year we were to say, "We will cut off all the rest and call it a day" it would be the fair thing to do. It sounds like an excellent thing to do, but would we not be bonusing-I was going to say something else-would we not be bonusing delay in paying one's bills when one can pay them? Perhaps, too, it might be a negative influence, by example, to those new veterans who are coming in under the Veterans Land Act.
I happen to know-and I shall take full responsibility for it, because I am speaking about my own constituency-of an old veteran who under the soldier settlement board came within the second category I mentioned a moment ago. Across the fence,
Supply-Veterans Affairs on the next farm, there came a veteran of the second world war who married, settled down and started in there. I know for a fact that, across the fence, the old timer said, whispering behind his hand, "Take it easy, my boy; at the other end you will be forgiven, the same as I am."
The amount placed in the estimates a year ago, and which is repeated this year, is in my opinion accomplishing the same thing more slowly but in a much better way. The hon. member for Battle River asked some questions which were made an order for return. I tabled the return today. His questions, and the answers to them, were as follows:
He asked first how many soldier settlers of great war I are still in debt to the soldier settlement board? His question was taken to mean September 30, the last date for which we have records, and the answer was that 1,950 are still in debt to the director of soldier settlement.
In his second question he asked the total amount of their indebtedness, and the answer showed an amount of $2,231,881.22.
The third question asked how many had paid off their loans and acquired clear titles since January 1, 1948. The reply was that there were 1,039.
The fourth question asked whether any reductions in debt had been granted during 1948 and 1949, and the reply was that there had been.
The fifth question asked, "If so, in how many cases, and what is the total amount of such reductions?" The answer was that there were 496 cases, to an amount of $182,515.83.
The last question asked as to (a) the smallest and (b) the largest reduction granted. The reply showed that the smallest was $18.25 and the largest $1,998.13.
From these answers it is apparent that even in a year and a bit we have been able to eliminate or to end the debt for a total of 496 old settlers. I hope that this year and perhaps next year the main task may be completed, and that the indebtedness of those who should be forgiven will be wiped off in that time.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
At eight o'clock we will carry on with public bills and orders for the first hour.
Will we proceed with veterans affairs estimates at nine o'clock?

Yes.

subtopic: PORTRAYAL OF CRIMES BY PICTURES IN MAGAZINES, ETC., TENDING TO INDUCE VIOLENCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, October 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fulton for the second reading of Bill No. 10, to amend the Criminal Code (portrayal of crimes).

subtopic: PORTRAYAL OF CRIMES BY PICTURES IN MAGAZINES, ETC., TENDING TO INDUCE VIOLENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on the bill this evening. I am glad that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is able to be here because I am sure he is much interested in the measure, and in the final analysis we shall have to look to him for help in having the bill put through the house.
I should like to point out that on the second reading of the bill we are only dealing with the principle, which is in effect that there should be an amendment to the Criminal Code making it a crime to print, publish, sell or distribute magazines commonly known as crime comics. So far in the debate every member who has spoken has been in favour of that principle. I was particularly struck by the speeches made by new members of the house. Several of them made their maiden speeches on this measure, and I thought that each of such speeches was excellent. It seemed to me that we were witnessing the house at its very best. It made one proud to be a member of the twenty-first parliament.
I believe the opinions expressed by the speakers who have taken part in the debate reflect the views of the Canadian people at large. No doubt most members have had representations from parent-teacher associations which, of course, are vitally interested in problems of this kind. There have also been representations from the national council of women and from the various Kiwanis clubs, which do such wonderful service work in all parts of the nation. In addition I have had representations from the university women's club of Vancouver who are very anxious that something should be done about the situation. Perhaps more important than all others, however, have been the representations from parents.
While the debate was in progress last night I received a letter from a mother in Vancouver who, by the way, is the daughter of a distinguished Canadian authoress, and I thought that she put the situation very clearly. She had heard over the radio of

the debate which took place last Tuesday evening, and she sat down and wrote a letter. It reads in part:
I know you are as anxious as any conscientious parent to see our Canadian children rescued from the evil effects of these criminal immoral magazines. I believe a big house-cleaning of our magazine and paper-back 25-cent books is overdue. We busy ourselves building youth centres, working in church to show our young people the guide posts to clean living, and all the time this stream of filthy books is allowed to come into our country.
In Canada we place as high a value on education as is done in any other country in the world. I believe that the same thing can be said about Scotland, and possibly other countries as well. Certainly every decent Canadian parent has as his or her first concern giving the children a start in life by seeing that they get a good education. I think that is typically Canadian. Parliament recognized the importance of children by enacting the family allowances legislation a few years ago. We place great value on pure food. We have many laws to make certain that nobody is given impure food. We show great determination in stamping out the drug traffic. I remember a few years ago the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), who was then minister of pensions and health, making a strong speech in the house on the dangers of marijuana, the use of which at that time was becoming quite prevalent in parts of Canada. We take drastic steps in other fields, and yet ye do nothing about this character poison. That is a good description for the crime comics.
We are all in favour of the principle of the bill, and I hope it will be passed. Once the bill is on the statute books it will be a strong deterrent and a warning to publishers all over Canada, and to the people who import these books from the United States, that they will be in trouble if they do not stop this traffic.
There is some suggestion that the bill may not be worded in exactly the right way. Actually the bill in its present form was not drawn by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). It is in a form suggested by the Right Hon. Mr. Ilsley when he was minister of justice. We could not have a finer authority on the wording of the bill. If it is not exactly right now it can be amended in committee. The point is that we are debating the principle of the bill, and I hope that the house will give it second reading.
Further, I hope there will be no delay. I am worried about that because of what happened to the bill amending the Criminal Code introduced by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) the other night. He had some good amendments although, mind you, I agree with the step taken by the

Minister of Justice (Mr. Gar son) when he said he would have the bill turned over to the commission revising the Criminal Code.
That was the proper step to take with that particular bill, but I am afraid that the Minister of Justice will come into the house, as soon as he is well again, and say that he is going to refer the present bill to the commission revising the Criminal Code. If that is done it will mean that the bill may not become law for a year. There will be no provision made at this session, and possibly not at the next session. A delay means not only an outpouring of more of this poison, but probably a speeding up of the process. The publishers of these magazines have a good thing. They are making money, and if they see they are going to have another six months or another year they are very apt to get out more of these comics and try to increase the circulation in order to cash in before it is too late.
Therefore I urge all members of the house, and particularly the Prime Minister, to realize the importance of prompt action on this particular measure. I suggest that we show the publishers of this junk that the House of Commons means business.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (St. John's West):
subtopic: PORTRAYAL OF CRIMES BY PICTURES IN MAGAZINES, ETC., TENDING TO INDUCE VIOLENCE
speechtext:
should like to join other hon. members in complimenting the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) on his initiative in bringing forward a bill of this kind. It seems to me that the most interesting subjects are brought up by private members, who also seem to win the approval of hon. members representing all parties in the house. It is interesting to find a discussion taking place on such a high moral plane as this one, and in this materialistic age it is consoling to find people so concerned about matters affecting the morals of our young people.
We are all in agreement as to the danger to the character of the youth of the land when their minds are poisoned by large doses of this evil kind of literature. Everyone feels that something should be done about it, but it is the hon. member for Kamloops who has brought forward this bill. Nevertheless I am wondering if he is going to accomplish what he has in mind by the amendment he proposes, and in support of that idea may I draw upon my experience as a judge in Newfoundland, as one who was especially interested in the problems of juvenile delinquency. For many years I took a special interest in that subject; and I am aware, as many hon. members have stated, that such books do have a certain effect upon the minds of young people. I think perhaps some are inclined to exaggerate that effect, and I doubt if they have as much effect as people think. However, they
Criminal Code
do have an effect upon young persons of weak minds or who, through bad associations, are prone to fall victims to the temptations which come to them through reading literature of that sort.
Two things, the movies and the comics, sometimes have a strong effect upon the minds of individuals; and I can recall several cases that came to my attention which in their way were really tragic. One was the case of a boy of good parentage who was before me on six charges of breaking and entering. He was only sixteen years of age. He told me that he had read about this in the comic books and that was how he came to go in for that sort of thing. I am glad to say that, later, when he became more mature, he turned out to be a good citizen. Another great tragedy occurred as the result of a boy seeing a hanging in a movie. He went home and experimented with a rope, and as a result killed himself. So there is no doubt that there are evil effects from both the movies and literature like these comics.
When one goes into a bookstore nowadays where magazines are displayed in great profusion, it seems to me they fall into three classes. There are the newspapers, which I suppose are the least harmful of all the literature displayed today. There are the magazines, which are in two classes: the kind dealing with economic and political subjects, and the kind dealing with true stories, true confessions, and that sort of thing. Then we have the comics. The children are interested only in the comics; but when an adult goes to a newsstand and sees the sort of picture magazines that are on display, he is ashamed to pick one up. I always consider it a reliable criterion of the sort of book that should not be permitted if it is the kind you are ashamed to let anyone, even a stranger, see you read.
We have been in confederation since April 1. One of the effects or results of confederation-I do not think it was intended by the Liberal party-has been to open the door to the sort of literature we are denouncing tonight. When we were more or less independent we had customs prohibitions which prevented these magazines from coming in, and the police and customs officials working together managed to keep out a great many of them. During the past summer, however, the country was flooded with magazines published in Toronto which were delivered through the post gratis. One day the assistant chief of police came to me in my office and said, "I don't know what I am going to do about these magazines. Everybody is complaining about them." I said, "I know what I am going to do; I am going to call the secretary for posts." I immediately

Criminal Code
called him and said, "Is it not an offence in Canada for this sort of literature to be sent through the mails?" He replied that it was. I told him what was happening, and he said he would take immediate steps to have it stopped.
As I read the section proposed by the hon. member, I understand that an offender is to be tried by a judge and jury. If that is not so, perhaps the hon. member will correct me.

subtopic: PORTRAYAL OF CRIMES BY PICTURES IN MAGAZINES, ETC., TENDING TO INDUCE VIOLENCE
speechtext:
It seems to me that procedure is too elaborate, and that this offence should be dealt with on summary conviction, or by ordinary summary trial. It also seems to me that if these magazines are imported from the United States the customs and postal authorities should be able to stop them, when they come within the category of books which are injurious to morals. If on the other hand they are published in this country the amendment to the act should give the police power to go in and take possession, by means of a warrant, of course, and the distributor should be dealt with by summary trial. If there is to be a trial by jury it is so long before the case is heard, and then when it comes up, with clever lawyers and that sort of thing, technicalities are likely to prevent the realization of what we have in mind, which is a procedure that will be summary and quick.
I do not intend to continue my comments at any great length, but there is one thing I should like to add. In Newfoundland we tried the interesting experiment of having a great public library system, furnished without cost by the government. For years we have had a libraries board which has been broadcasting programs about books and reading all over the country. We have twenty-seven or twenty-eight regional libraries all over Newfoundland, each with books especially chosen for children. I think my hon. friends opposite who come from Newfoundland will bear with me when I say that this comic book evil rarely reached the outports of Newfoundland but is confined to the city of St. John's and two or three of the larger places such as Corner Brook, Grand Falls and Bell Island. It does not reach into the smaller settlements, thank God. Instead of the comic books, therefore, we have the other books which are carefully chosen by the special selection committee of the libraries board. We have attacked the problem in that way; and in our public library in St. John's, where we have a large selection of good children's books of all kinds, those books are used extensively and it has been a great success. I believe the existence of the public library system has 
helped a great deal in mitigating the evil to which reference has been made here.
As hon. members have suggested, I believe the practical approach to the problem consists in placing good literature before the boys and girls and stressing it continuously in radio programs and articles in the press. This will probably do as much as, if not more than, legislation of the sort suggested in this bill. At the same time, however, when an obvious evil exists I believe it is the duty of parliament to put it down by some statutory enactment.
On motion of Mr. Cardiff, the debate was adjourned.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
526.	Departmental administration, $2,157,024.

Mr. Chairman, if the committee agrees, we might proceed item by item and as we come to the proper items I shall attempt to cover those points raised in the debate this afternoon.
Before doing so, however, and to complete what I was saying before the recess about the question raised by the member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) regarding the steps taken to adjust old debts and clear titles, may I say that matter will receive the careful consideration of the deputy minister and the director of the soldier settlement board.

Item agreed to.
527.	District administration, $2,945,528.

I should like to ask the minister about the Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act. The annual report concerning this act for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1949, shows that there have been loans totalling $7,517,879.85; of that amount nearly half or $3,372,754.87 has been repaid. I believe this is a splendid record. The report also shows that only 34 claims have been defaulted, amounting to $36,686.05. Those figures reflect great credit on the veterans.
There is nothing in the report, however, to show the number of applications for loans which were turned down. Could the minister supply that information?

The total number of applications not approved for the purchase of a business amounts to fourteen; for the purchase of an interest in a partnership, five; for the purchase of tools and equipment, three; for repairing tools and equipment, etc., one; for the construction and repair of buildings, five; for the purchase of a motorized

unit, seven. This makes a total of thirty-five in all categories which were not approved.
Has there been any demand for loans by veterans who wish to buy into a private company? As the law reads now a veteran can only buy into a partnership.
None have come to my attention. All applications so far could be covered by the purchase into a partnership.

Item agreed to.
528.	Veterans welfare services (formerly rehabilitation services), $3,686,711.

There are one or two questions I should like to ask about this item. First, I believe an order in council was passed a few days ago amending the rehabilitation act so that personnel in hospitals would receive training allowances or something of that nature. Could the minister explain what those changes mean? I believe the order in council was dated September 28, 1949.
The second point is concerned with the transfer from university training to vocational training and vice versa. I believe there was a deadline set when applications for transfer from one type of training to the other had to be made. I think it was within six months of the termination of the course. Some people did not receive any notice about that deadline. The only notices which were sent out appeared in the newspapers and, quite obviously, many veterans would miss them. People who were travelling or who lived in isolated parts of the country would not see such a notice. Would the minister consider extending that deadline in cases where a recommendation was made, perhaps by the president of the university or the principal of the vocational training course concerned, so that the men who had given up hope of being able to transfer from vocational training to university might still be able to take advantage of that amendment. They would then be able to continue a course which, perhaps, they had given up because they saw no opportunity of following the line of rehabilitation they particularly desired.
I have in mind men who were taking a course in carpentry who felt they would like to go farther and take a course in architecture at a university. When we are dealing with this item, would the minister answer the questions which were directed to him before the recess regarding the rehabilitation of the men who served in the merchant navy?

On the first point, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I have not a copy of that order in council before me. I shall bring it with me at some later date when these estimates are being considered. On the
Supply-Veterans Affairs question of the changeover of training, and the arrangements that were made to make that more flexible, I can say now that if a given veteran, through circumstances beyond his control, did not get the information with regard to that change in time to get in under the dateline, then the matter will certainly be taken into consideration to see that he does not suffer on that account. I doubt whether there is anything I can add tonight with respect to the matter that was discussed before the parliamentary committee and at the last session with regard to the merchant marine. As was pointed out this afternoon, the committee at that time recommended that the younger men who served in the merchant marine should be given the opportunity for vocational training in addition to training in their own business at sea. It was pointed out that at our seaports on each coast some of these young men were not working but were hanging around and being subjected to subversive influences; and it was suggested that it would be a good thing if they could be allowed to take vocational training in the same way as those who had served in the armed forces.
This matter was considered by the government, and the Department of Transport arranged that this be done, going through my department; the training was carried on in conjunction with the vocational training centres of the province in the same way as it was carried on with the veterans. More recently representations have been made, to the same effect as those that were made this afternoon, that the age of thirty was considered too young. Many of these men had already gone beyond that age and still were not permanently employed. On behalf of the Minister of Transport I think I can state that the matter will be carefully considered in view of what was said this afternoon.

There is one matter that I should again like to bring to the attention of the minister, namely, the plight of one group of the auxiliary services that I feel have had a shabby deal. I refer to the Red Cross girls. As the minister well knows, they did not get even a clothing allowance when they came back to Canada. As a result of the small amount of remuneration received, and on which they had to live while overseas, when they came out of the service they had nothing. I wish the minister would give serious consideration to this matter.

I should like to ask the minister to give the committee a short explanation of the position of a Newfoundland veteran now coming under the veterans legislation with respect to vocational training. Will his rights for vocational training have lapsed

Supply-Veterans Affairs before the act came into force in Newfoundland or will he have some retroactive rights to training?

As all hon. members know, including those from Newfoundland, veterans in Newfoundland are in all respects now in receipt of the benefits under the veterans charter in the same manner as though Newfoundland had been a part of Canada at the time of demobilization. I think that is a fair statement. To refer to vocational training and university training, I may say that in all parts of Canada at the present time the main body of veterans have had their training. As to university training, Newfoundland had a plan of their own. They also had a plan for vocational training. It was somewhat different from ours, but it was a good plan. Some of these veterans were in receipt of training when union took place. My department took them over and carried them on under our rights until they finished their particular training, whether it was vocational or university training.

Before this item is passed, I think utterance should be given to a word of commendation of a certain type of public servant. We are free, and properly so, to criticize where criticism is due; and I think we should give praise where praise is due. I refer to the type commonly known in the small towns as the D.V.A. representative. I believe that later on he was attached to the Department of Labour but he originally came to towns the size of mine as a D.V.A. representative. I should like to say to the minister that in those places with which I am familiar these men have done a job which it is impossible to extol too highly. The veterans of all services-even veterans who politically have no use for this government, and many who have not much use for the economic system under which we live-are all loud in their praise of the D.V.A. local representative who had assisted in matters such as employment, the Veterans Land Act, loans and so on. I think that some of us-and I am glad to do so -should publicly express our appreciation of the work these men have done on behalf of all veterans.

It gives me great pleasure to direct those welcome remarks to my colleague the Minister of Labour, inasmuch as this official who has just been spoken of is in reality an employee of the offices of the national employment service across Canada. It is true that some of them did happen to serve previously in the Department of Veterans Affairs. To what has been said I should like to add that, in every centre of Canada where there is an office of the Department of Veterans Affairs and also an office of the

national employment service, I believe the closest liaison and co-operation have been carried out in order to obtain employment for our veterans.
Can the minister give the number of persons on the staff and the number of patients at the health and occupational centre at Billings Bridge?
That was the subject of an order for return, Mr. Chairman. Was the hon. member's question with reference to all of them or just with reference to the one?
Just the one.
In the Rideau health and occupational centre there are 118 patients at the present time.
What is the number of persons on the staff?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That information was tabled in an order for return the other day. I will try to find it.
I will get that information for the hon. member in a few minutes.

The minister stated that further consideration will be given to a change in the provision under which a merchant seaman gets vocational training. Can he explain to the committee just how the authority is divided on that question between the Department of Transport and the Department of Veterans Affairs? I have just recently had the case of a merchant seaman brought to my attention. Of course he is unable to get university training. Nevertheless, he has gone to university and requires only one more year to get the degree of bachelor of commerce. In the meantime he has applied for vocational training in the way of articling to a chartered accountant. After graduating from university he proposes to take up chartered accountancy. He could get that vocational training from the Department of Transport, but they say that if he is to get it he must start in right away with his articles. Obviously it is foolish for him not to finish his course at the university. The Department of Transport refuses to give him a year's extension on the vocational training. I do not think that is right. The Department of Veterans Affairs is obviously quite willing to let him have that extension. The minister's own department obviously believes that this lad should be allowed to finish his course at university and then get the vocational training but the Department of Transport officials are making an arbitrary ruling that they will not give him that vocational training unless he leaves university to commence his articles. There is a division of authority which is unfortunate. I suggest that the Department

of Veterans Affairs be given full authority to deal with these applications. I can see that the establishing of his service in the merchant navy would be done through the Department of Transport but once he had established that service, why not let the Department of Veterans Affairs take over from then on? The way it is now these lads are not getting a fair deal.
Further, does the minister not think that the merchant navy men should now be allowed to get educational training as well as vocational training? In the meantime many of them have paid their own way through perhaps two or three years but they are still in university. It is a shame that they have not had that educational help.

I will answer the last question first by saying that a parliamentary committee composed of many minds did not recommend the university training and it has not been put into effect. To answer the other question, in their service with the merchant marine these men were under the Department of Transport. If the occasion should arise and the merchant navy were ever increased again, I presume the same situation would exist. It is also true that the Department of Transport have all the records available regarding these men; we have not.
Regarding their service?

Regarding their service in the merchant navy. Consequently it seemed sound, and I think it is, to have their applications made to the Department of Transport. If by chance they came to my department or to the district offices they were routed through the Department of Transport to decide upon their eligibility under the terms that had been laid down. After that had been decided upon and they were accepted for training they were sent on to the Department of Veterans Affairs to carry on their vocational training in the regular vocational training courses throughout the districts. As to responsibility during that stage, we have looked upon it as a joint one. If my hon. friend feels that injustices have been done in individual cases I know that my colleague, the Minister of Transport, would be glad to discuss it with him, as I would be.
I would rather discuss it with you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: May I answer the question asked a moment ago with respect to the Rideau hospital? The staff is 103; the potential patient capacity is 175. At the time the return was made a week ago there were 118 patients in the hospital.

Item agreed to.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
529.	Treatment services, $34,478,808.

I should like to ask the
minister two or three questions in connection with the scale of fees charged to veterans who are not eligible for free hospitalization in the departmental hospitals. Hon. members will recall that a considerable amount of discussion took place on this last spring or the year before, and a number of cases were brought up that have frequently been charged up to $9 a day for care in one of the departmental hospitals. What is the average of fees now being charged? Has there been any change during the last year? If not, is any change contemplated? As the minister knows, so far as hospital accommodation is concerned, in many places it is very difficult. If those fees were charged at any time with the idea in mind of not competing with private hospitals, it certainly does not apply to many places at the present time. Frequently the only hospital that a veteran is able to get into is a veterans hospital. No beds are vacant in the ordinary hospitals in the places in which the veterans happen to live. Whatever charge is made, if it is necessary to make a charge to the veteran who can afford it I quite agree with it; but the veteran who is not able to afford it is in a different position. In any event, if he has to be charged, the charge ought to be made as low as possible to cover whatever extra cost is necessary to hospitalize that veteran in a bed which perhaps otherwise would not be occupied.

Fees are sometimes referred to as merely the matter of bed and board within the hospital. Then there is the larger service of the bed and board within the hospital, medical service, X-rays and so forth which come under an all-inclusive rate, including everything within the hospital. That averages $9.75.
Does that all-inclusive rate include surgical operations?
Yes, everything.
Has there been any change in the rate in the last year? Is that the same rate that has been in effect more or less since the beginning?
The average has increased by 75 cents. It has increased from $9 to $9.75 in the last year.

Can the minister tell us what the basis of that is? Why is it necessary to charge $9.75, which I think he will realize is beyond the means of a large number of veterans? Their incomes just do not warrant a cost of $9.75 a day for hospitalization.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
I assure the hon. member that a profit is not being made. It is considered to be not greater than the cost, and I am informed that a number of civilian hospitals charge more than that rate.

I can quite believe that a number of civilian hospitals may charge more. The point I am getting at is this. The hospital is there in operation, and if this bed were not being occupied by the veteran who is not entitled to free hospital treatment, in practically all cases it would not be occupied at all, because these people get in only if the veterans who are entitled to hospitalization have not filled the hospital. The rate, I take it, is based on the total cost of running the hospital. Whether it includes depreciation on the capital invested I do not know, but 1 would take it that that is so. If that is so, I would suggest that it is not necessary; that the hospitalization of these veterans, particularly those of limited means, could be done on a very much smaller fee than would be charged in the ordinary hospital.

I can assure the hon. member that there is no amount tucked in that $9.75 to cover capital investment. The other point which I probably should make clear is that we are not able to have a non-veteran who is not eligible for treatment come in as a patient. Those who are charged that amount are veterans sent to our hospitals by such organizations as provincial or municipal governments, or organizations such as the Canadian paraplegic association, and others who pay the amount on behalf of the veteran patient.
How much revenue has the department secured from that source during the past year?
I have not the information here, but I shall get it.

It does not seem fair that the Department of Veterans Affairs should charge that amount for a veteran going into hospital, in view of the fact that the Indian affairs branch pays only $3 or $3.50 a day for an Indian in hospital. There is something wrong somewhere, definitely. I know of veterans who have had to go to hospital and who, instead of going to veterans hospitals and paying $9 a day, have found it cheaper to go to local hospitals.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. member know of an instance where a veteran has, out of his own money, paid $9.75 per day?
Yes; I have had cases where they have gone to local hospitals instead of paying that amount.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: But does the hon. member know of any case where a veteran has paid out that amount?
The parliamentary assistant told us that they paid it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
No, we did not. We said that there is a charge there, but that in almost every instance where $9.75 has been collected it has been collected on behalf of a veteran who was there as a charge against a third party. These are veterans who are hospitalized at the request of municipalities or other organizations, or perhaps as a result of an accident where the claim lies against a third party.
I believe that upon examination the hon. member would find that there are exceedingly few cases where the veteran himself has ever paid that charge. I would be interested to know of any cases where a veteran has actually been there over a period of time, and paid that much.
From what came out during the last session, and the preceding one, and from the fact that the minister said they were charging $9 or $9.50 a day, I know that is so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: There is a liability of that; I believe that would be a better way to express it.
Yes, but every veteran feels that is what he would have to pay if he went into hospital. He does everything possible to avoid the hospital on account of that charge.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Believe me, he does everything possible to get in.

No, to keep away from it. While I am on my feet I would ask whether the department has tried out, for blind veterans, the electric eye which has been used by the service departments in the United States. These weigh about four pounds and project a beam of light in front of the veteran. When the light beam is broken by an object in the user's path a warning is given by the vibration it produces. I understand this has worked out very well, and I was wondering if this department had done anything about it?
I understand the department has been in touch with the situation through Colonel Baker of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, and that the matter is being studied.

I believe I could supply the parliamentary assistant with the names of individuals who have been in the veterans hospital at Victoria. I cannot say for certain, but I believe they paid the money themselves. Certainly they were billed for it. Then,

before they were cured, they moved from the veterans hospital to the Royal Jubilee hospital at Victoria.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The stated liability is there. But there is a latitude with respect to collection which has not, in my experience, worked any real hardship on anyone who could not pay it. I asked the question, not with the suggestion that there is no liability; there is. I have indicated however that the administration is such that it does not, in my opinion, work any hardship.

I should like to comment on what was said a short time ago by the parliamentary assistant. I brought it out because I had three complaints within the last two months from individuals who thought they were being charged more than they should have been in the veterans hospital-certainly far more than they had anticipated having to pay.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It could happen that either the hon. member who has just spoken or myself, both veterans, might as a result of an emergency be admitted. I believe he would agree, as would other hon. members in the committee, that under the circumstances either of us would be able to pay for that accommodation. Under those conditions it would probably be collected in full. But my point is that there is no insistence against a veteran who needs treatment and is ill-equipped to pay it, just because the liability does exist.

The statement has been made that veterans would prefer to go to hospitals other than veterans hospitals. That is not the fact. Along with many other hon. members of the house, I am a member of the Canadian Legion. We believe the department is doing its best to provide for the veterans. I do not believe in my experience with the Legion in the Vancouver area that there has ever been a case where a veteran has definitely decided to go to some hospital other than Shaughnessy. I do know of some boys in Shaughnessy who have not been able to pay for their hospital accommodation for some time. One of the boys I visited the day before I came east is dying of tuberculosis. His hospital rate is $9.75 a day, but he will never be expected to pay it. And the hon. member who asks that question very well knows it.
No one is fairer to the veterans than is this department, whether it be in hospitalization or in any other particular. I resent the implication that the department would ask the veteran in hospital to pay the $9.75, if he were unable to pay it.

Is there any possibility of men of the merchant navy getting hospitalization? At the present time they are not entitled to any hospitalization whatsoever unless they happen to be pensioners, and there are very few pensioners among them because the pension provisions are too strict. It is not possible to give these men hospitalization? Surely they can at least get that. It does not come under the Department of Transport. This question can be settled by the Department of Veterans Affairs. I urge the minister to make some provision to allow these men to get hospitalization. It is very unfair that they cannot get into the veterans hospitals.

Of course, under existing legislation the answer to that is no. It is in reality a part of a larger question. As the hon. member knows, there was not only this group of non-veterans, technically speaking, but also a number of others who were considered by the parliamentary committee, and the principle has not been acknowledged that they are entitled to the benefits, including hospitalization, that were provided under the veterans charter for those who served in the armed forces.

Is it not a fact that no amendment of any legislation would be required to give them hospitalization? Hospitalization is provided by order in council. No amendment to any statute is required.

There is a similar situation with regard to the widows of men who were drawing the war veterans allowance. They come under the War Veterans Allowance Act and yet they are not entitled to hospitalization. I believe they are the only group coming under the War Veterans Allowance Act who cannot get hospitalization. In my opinion that is also an injustice. The minister was going to get me the figure of the amount of revenue that had been taken in by the department through the fees I referred to. Has he got that now?

I will attempt to get that exactly.
