533. War veterans allowance board-administration, $237,204.
The minister did not make any reply to the suggestions which were made this afternoon concerning war veterans allowance. Will he make a reply now?

I think the main discussion this afternoon was about the adequacy of the war veterans allowance as it exists at the present time following the increase which was made last year. The other point which was discussed was the question whether ex-members of the forces who served with the United Kingdom, with the British commonwealth of nations, or our allies, and who have lived in Canada for a period of time, should be eligible under the act. Dealing with the first point, as hon. members know, only a year ago the amount of the allowance was increased from $30 to $40 per month for single men and from $60 to $70 per month for married men. That was put into effect last spring but was retroactive to the first of October of the year before. I should like to mention, in case it is overlooked, that when we come to the amount under war veterans allowance and pensions it will be necessary for hon. members to note that in last year's estimates it covers the whole of last year plus the preceding six months, which makes it a little larger than it otherwise would be. During the summer it appeared to us that there were veterans, particularly in the cities and towns, who were undergoing hardship because they had no other means of support and were not employable. Welfare workers within our department made a test for our own information in a number of centres across Canada to find out just what the situation was. We were very happy to see that conditions were not as bad as we sometimes feared they might be, but on the other hand we did find that hardship was being experienced particularly in the cities. That was the reason why I put forward a request last spring that there be inserted in the estimates an item for half a million dollars in order that we could continue and complete the survey quietly and steadily, and while so doing do something to overcome the hardship which our survey showed did exist.
We did find that some of the old veterans, who had become eligible for war veterans allowance and were getting a cheque every month, did not read the newspapers very much, or the periodicals of the veterans associations. As a result we found that when something happened to their teeth and they had to get them out they went to the dentist and paid him for pulling them; or if they had to go to a doctor for some medicine, they took their few dollars from the war veterans allowance and paid for it. In other words

they did not know they were entitled to medical assistance under the War Veterans Allowance Act.
That situation, of course, was easily corrected. There are many other ways in which by advice and consultation conditions may be improved without too much difficulty. Later on I shall be able to give the exact figures; but in setting up this fund we desired that it should have a degree of flexibility which would enable our welfare people in the district to work in direct co-operation with the welfare people of the community in order to meet without too much delay any cases of hardship which might arise. On the whole in spite of some of the criticism we heard this afternoon I think that this is being done. We have kept in close touch with the situation here in Ottawa. A committee headed by my deputy minister has managed that fund from Ottawa, but a great deal of discretion has been left to those in the field to deal with local situations without delay when the need has been established. It was also necessary to have a good deal of flexibility geographically, because all veterans across the country are not making application for assistance from this fund in the same degree. In my own end of the country the applications are comparatively few. In British Columbia the number of applications and approvals is very high. That is due to the fact that many of our old veterans have gone west because of the climate, and have settled down in that well known paradise of Vancouver island. There they are, and there they foregather.
I do take exception to the suggestion advanced this afternoon that a severe additional means test is being applied in connection with the war veterans allowance. I have spoken to a good many of these men, and in my experience they have no objection whatever to going to the official in our district office, who knows all about them anyway because he has all the information in the files, and saying to that official, "Here are some additional circumstances that have got us into trouble. Can we get some additional help?" It is just as simple as that. It is not a means test piled upon another means test. D.V.A. people who conducted this voluntary survey, taking a few here and a few there, did not go out as inspectors or as a gestapo to find out whether these people were hiding something under the mattress. They went out to sit down with the recipients of this allowance, to discuss their problems and find out what could be done to help. That is the spirit in which this additional amount called the war veterans allowance assistance fund has been and is being administered. By the end of the fiscal year I am
Supply-Veterans Affairs sure we will be able to tell whether this amount will be sufficient or whether further steps should be taken. I would like to carry on until the end of the year in order to ascertain these facts.

Very recently another matter was brought to my attention to which I think the minister might give a little attention. I understand that a person receiving the war veterans allowance is held down to an income of $1,100 a year, including that allowance. If he is in receipt of casual earnings, however, I do not believe that figure applies. If a man has a steady job, though it may not be worth very much, he has a ceiling placed upon his earnings. I have particular reference to the case of a man who is seventy-two years old this month. The druggist in his town needed some help for about four hours a day, and this man undertook to fill the position, for which he is paid $7.50 per week or approximately $30 a month. Apparently he was earning that money for some little time before the war veterans allowance board found out about it, and now they have reduced his allowance until a certain amount has been repaid.
I believe something should be done about a case like that, where a man of this age had enough ambition to go out and make a few extra dollars. He told me that he and his wife could not live in comfort on the allowance he was receiving, so he was trying to get a little extra money. I do not think it should make any difference whether it is a steady job or casual earnings. Perhaps in this case that $7.50 a week might be classed as casual earnings.

I should like a chance to study the case mentioned by my hon. friend, but from what he has said I take it that this man is permanently employed, with so much money coming in regularly every week. Consequently that would be looked upon by the board as a salary or wage. I think hon. members know that we have interpreted the expression "casual earnings" in very broad fashion, but I do not think we could interpret it broadly enough to include the case mentioned by my hon. friend, if I understood him correctly.
Then I wonder if it would not be better for that man to give up his steady job and work every other week, or something like that. Would that make a difference?

I can hardly answer that question. The amount earned is above that permitted by the act, and whether or not it would pay him to make a change would be, of course, up to him. I imagine he is rather proud of the fact that he is able to earn that

Supply-Veterans Affairs much money under his own power. I shall be glad to look into the case fully with my hon. friend.

Then I wonder if the minister would suggest that he apply for the amount which was made available last year, of up to $15 a month, provided he stops work. Many other people throughout the country have done that. He would then get away from this steady salary, and make application for that extra amount provided last year.
I shall be glad to discuss the case with my hon. friend.

Do I understand from the minister's statement that in every case this additional allowance is in the nature of a grant of one kind or another rather than a definite increase in the amount of the war veterans allowance received each month?

It is an amount utilized in an attempt to overcome special hardship which may be immediate or of some duration. It may be a spot amount of $50. It may be an amount to be advanced over a period of two months or six months or twelve months. It is flexible enough to enable those administering it to use discretion, and I feel that it is in the nature of an auxiliary to the regular war veterans allowance, and is accomplishing quite a good deal in proportion to the amount of money expended.
Then would the veteran have to apply each year?

The veteran would be in close touch with those administering it. In some cases it might not be necessary to do so, but I would imagine in most cases it would be necessary for our administrator in the district to know about the case from time to time.

That brings up the objectionable feature, Mr. Chairman, that this is only a temporary measure. In most cases, it is not even for a year. Next year if a veteran is to get the same benefit he will have to re-apply. I believe some more permanent arrangement will have to be made. If the minister is only trying this out for the remainder of the present fiscal year, there is not much objection to it. However, if this is the manner in which assistance is to be given year in and year out, then certainly some better means of doing it will have to be found. If a veteran receiving assistance only gets it temporarily, and has to apply each year, he may receive one amount this year and a different amount next year.
He might not need it next year.
If that is a permanent policy, I do not think it is sound. Something better than that will have to be worked out, and I feel sure the minister will agree with me in that contention.

I am sure I did not indicate that that was anything approaching a permanent policy. The regular recipient of war veterans allowance under the act is not, by any means, necessarily permanent in the same way a pensioner might be permanent. Under our present act, the case must be reviewed from time to time and changes made based upon the conditions under which the veteran is living. This year I believe we are really more closely in touch with those in receipt of aid than we are with the regular recipients. As I pointed out before, I think it is revealing a number of things, and by the end of the first fiscal year we shall have acquired more information on that subject than we have had heretofore.

The situation with regard to old age pensions is not being met at all by this temporary provision. In British Columbia the old age pensioner is receiving $50 per month, and that increase is not temporary. The burnt-out pension is supposed to be the equivalent of the old age pension, as the minister stated in his speech I quoted this afternoon. In British Columbia and some of the other provinces the situation will develop where the old age pensioner will receive more than a war veterans allowance recipient. I do suggest to the minister that the war veterans allowance will have to be made equal to the old age pension. The idea of having a temporary increase is not going to meet the situation at all, particularly in view of the fact that the old age pensioner now receives more than the war veterans allowance recipient.
I still come back to the point that the old age pensioner and his wife have to be seventy years of age before they can receive a pension.
It is a rather weak excuse.

I should like to make a few remarks on the question discussed by the member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). In talking to recipients of war veterans allowance, I find they have mainly three grievances. The first, of course, is that the allowance is too small. Second, before special assistance is given an investigation is made, and that is deeply resented. This is the matter referred to by the member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) and by other members on a number of occasions, namely, the means test.

I would suggest to the minister, and through him to the government, that if the means test is to be continued we should pay the allowance until the income reached the amount exempted under the Income Tax Act, $1,000 for single persons and $2,000 for married persons. The recipients of the allowance would be permitted to earn as much as they could, and if they exceeded these exemptions they could be taxed in the ordinary way, including the amount received from the war veterans allowance. I believe it would be the least costly way of handling it. There must be an enormous expenditure of time and money in making these investigations. Investigations are irritating, there is no doubt about it. I am informed by individuals in receipt of the war veterans allowance that these investigations are conducted by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Some means will have to be found of getting rid of these petty annoyances.
In British Columbia we are faced with the fact that the old age pension proper plus the supplementary amount paid by the government now totals approximately $50 per month. When both recipients are over the age of seventy, it is considerably more than married persons receive under the War Veterans Allowance Act. I do not think the fact that an applicant is seventy years of age should make any difference. It takes as much money to keep a couple who are sixty as it does to keep a couple who are seventy.
They would eat more.

I would imagine they would because the younger couple would be more active and expect more of life than those who had reached a more advanced age. I would suggest to the minister that he take these matters under consideration and see if there is some way we can eliminate these petty annoyances to people who are in a difficult position in many cases, through no fault of their own.
Could the minister tell me in what circumstances a veteran who is drawing a disability pension must find himself before he would be entitled to receive assistance from the army benevolent fund?

The terms of reference for the army benevolent fund were worked out by a parliamentary committee. As a result of that, an independent board was created which worked out its own regulations and technique. It is responsible to parliament in a general way through the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I would not be able to answer a hypothetical question with regard to a pensioner, but I am quite sure he could receive funds from the army benevolent fund if the situation warranted it.

Will the minister, after giving the matter some thought, give the house a justification for the present means test against the veterans who are drawing the war veterans allowance? I should like to know by what process of reasoning that sum of money was arrived at by the men who originally fixed it at the present amount.
I have never been able to see any sense in it at all. What can be the object of the Department of Veterans Affairs in wanting to keep the veterans on a subsistence level, in constant and appalling need? I fail to see any sensible objective. I can understand why the Department of Veterans Affairs would want to keep the veterans allowance down as low as possible in order to avoid expense, and that seems to be their primary objective. But why they should object to people who receive the war veterans allowance going out and making more where they can do so, I never could see, especially when the sum is as meagre as that which now constitutes the means test for veterans receiving the war veterans allowance in Canada. After the minister has had time to think this matter over, I should like to have him justify before the committee and before the country the amount of the means test at the present time.

Even though it may not be what the hon. member for Lethbridge wants, I suppose the correct answer is that we are administering an act, and in that act appears this item called the means test. We try to administer it fairly and in accordance with what we think is the will of the people who passed the act; and they were the members of this house representing the people of Canada. I do not intend to go behind that and try to enter into the minds of those who inserted the means test into the act when it was placed upon the statute books.

I can understand that, Mr. Chairman. But I should like to know whether this means test was forced on the Department of Veterans Affairs; and if so, I should like to know who it was that forced it on them. The means test is said to have been passed by this house, but it was introduced by a government and passed by this house because it was introduced by a government. I am positive that no members of this house ever told the government that they wanted to have that means test so meagre as it is at the present time. If there is any way of finding out who it was that first conceived setting that means test down at as low a level as it now is, I should like to find out who it was and why he did it.

The means test was not forced upon the Department of Veterans Affairs

Supply-Veterans Affairs any more than it was forced upon the Department of National Health and Welfare with regard to the old age pension. It is part of the legislation which was considered and passed by parliament. That was one of the sections within that legislation, just as it is one of the sections within the old age pension legislation. I do not think there is anything more that I can say on that subject tonight.

As I see it, the point is this. It was considered by parliament because somebody designed the thing and brought it down to parliament. What I should like to know is who that fellow was who designed it, and why he designed it in the way he did. That is the thing.

I do not want to continue this discussion, but the first designing was done away back in 1929 and 1930. In the spring of 1930 the first bill covering war veterans allowances was brought in. This item was in that original act. The act has been amended a number of times since then, but this item remains in it. I know that it has been discussed, but it remains in it because apparently the majority of the members of this parliament felt that it should be in it.

Would it not be more accurate to say that that is the way the majority of the members of the treasury board felt? I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the time is long overdue when a complete revision is brought about in this parliament. I suggest that the minister take this matter up in the cabinet and tell them that that is what the people all over this country think.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I do not want to detract from this all-out attack on the means test as a whole. But since the minister is to look out and see if he can find this fellow who first invented it, may I ask a susidiary question. The minister will recall that this afternoon I was discussing the way in which the war veterans allowance means test with respect to liquid assets is meaner in its application than is the case with the old age pension people. I should like to know whether the provision which says that a veteran must reduce his liquid assets to a certain amount before he can qualify for burnt-out pension is in the act or is in the regulations under the act.
The point brought up by my hon. friend is not a part of the act. It is a ruling by the board administering or interpreting the act.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Now we have something about which something could be done. When the minister can say that the point we are

kicking about, such as the whole means test, is in the act he can say that, as long as the majority think as the majority does in this parliament, nothing can be done. But here is something that is done not by virtue of the act itself but by virtue of an administrative ruling or regulation made under the act. I am sure that the majority of members of this house, if they had a chance to express themselves, would say that the way of administering the means test in connection with the burnt-out pension should be no more strict in any respect than it is with regard to the old age pension. I am not going to ask the minister to make any promise or commitment here and now, but I hope he will look into the matter. In other words, the veteran is asked to spend it or dissipate it or he is asked to live a little bit beyond what he feels he should because of his assets, in the hope that he will get the allowance later on.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I remind the minister that there have been visiting in Ottawa this week women representing the non-pensioned veterans' widows association. I have no doubt they have seen him if they found it possible to get an audience. He knows some of the requests they have been making from time to time. One is that they should be granted treatment provisions, hospitalization and so on. He also knows about their particular plea that England be treated as a theatre of war with respect to world war I. Have they been able to make any dent upon him during the course of this week in connection with those matters?

I have had the pleasure on two occasions this week of meeting with the ladies referred to. I should like to state

also that these ladies told me that they had seen rumours in the press that the government had taken steps, or was about to take steps, on this much discussed matter affecting veterans who had served in the United Kingdom forces or in British commonwealth forces, which of course would in turn affect the widows of those veterans. I regret very much if such rumours went out because the facts of the matter are these, as has been pointed out. I did indicate to veterans organizations that I would study the matter. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra referred to that. I can assure him that that promise has been kept. There are matters relating to it which I discussed with the ladies and which the hon. member for York-ton referred to in passing this afternoon. The greater number of those from the commonwealth who served in a theatre of war, and who have been in the country for twenty years, came from Scotland, England, Ireland, north and south-and there, if you say in your definition "from the commonwealth", what are you going to do about the south of Ireland? That is only a minor problem. It is not an insuperable one. I have a record of some who have served in battle in the forces of Australia and New Zealand, but they are not anything like-
How many?

I do not know how many, but I know there are a few. Then, if we are to study the problem of these people as we have been doing, shall we make a clean job of it and include all those who served on our side between 1914 and 1918? When you go on from there you have the United States, France, Belgium, Japan, Italy, Russia and quite a number of other countries. I have the list upstairs, which indicates that at least I have been giving it some study. The figures that have been estimated so far indicate that there might be in the vicinity of 2,000 British commonwealth people in the country who might be eligible in this connection. That is only a very rough guess.
Two thousand?

Yes, from the British commonwealth, who might be eligible; not those who are in the country. There is a larger number than that in the country. Other steps are under way to try at least to find out some similar estimate as to those of allied and associated countries who may be in this country. All that I will say tonight in response to the question is that the matter is being studied by my department and by the government.

I do not expect that it will be completed in time to bring in any legislation at this session.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I take it that the question of the widows of Canadian veterans who saw service only in England in world war I is included in this whole study.

No, it is not, because I do not think anybody has ever made more clear the principle underlying the war veterans allowance than did the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra this afternoon. The whole principle of this bill today, as it was in 1930, is that it is designed for those who had service in battle and because of that service in battle may have become pre-aged, burnt out, and consequently were entitled to a ten-year differential as compared with an old age civilian Canadian who had served his country not in uniform. If that principle were done away with, I think it would be almost as reasonable to say that Canada was a theatre of war in both world war I and world war II as to say that England was a theatre of war in world war I.

In view of the minister's
promise to look into the question of liquid assets I bring one aspect of it to his attention. A certain amount of liquid assets is allowed and at the same time a man is permitted to own a property or a house up to the value of $4,000.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Assessed value?

From time to time cases have been brought to my attention where the wife of a man dies and he is left a house which is perhaps larger than he is able to look after because he is a widower. In any event, he has to readjust his custom of life. He sells the house. That increases his assets by approximately $4,000. He may be waiting until he can find a smaller house, until he gets married again, or until he can make certain adjustments, but he loses his war veterans allowance. I do not suppose he loses it immediately but very shortly afterwards, until such time as the money which has accrued from the sale of his property has been reduced to the amount of liquid assets which he is permitted to hold. Therefore he has no chance of ever again having a house of his own. In the years to come, should he get married again, he has no opportunity of buying a house. If the minister intends to look into the question of the amount of liquid assets, might that point be taken into consideration? A widower has been left with increased assets owing to the sale of his house. He should be able to retain these-I am not going to say indefinitely-for a reasonable length of time until

Supply-Veterans Affairs he can get his living arrangements adjusted, buy a new property or get established in some other way.
We shall be glad to look into that.

There is no doubt that veterans across Canada do resent, and I think quite bitterly, the fact that civilians can get a higher rate of pension under the Old Age Pensions Act than the veteran can under the War Veterans Allowance Act. The minister has pointed out to us that the veterans can get the war veterans allowance at 60, a lower age than would qualify a civilian for old age pension; but he himself has reminded us of the fact that that was done in the first instance because the veteran was pre-aged by ten years. That being the case, it is not fair to refer to the fact that veterans can get war veterans allowance at a lower age.
Following along the line of the minister's discussion, would he suggest that when a war veteran and his wife receiving the benefit of the War Veterans Allowance Act reach the age of 70 he would be better off to drop the war veterans allowance and seek a pension under the Old Age Pensions Act? I am sure the minister himself would admit that it would not be a happy situation were our veterans recommended to drop their help under soldier legislation and seek it under civilian legislation merely because they can get a higher pension. Yet that is the situation that exists today, and many veterans have come to me and pointed out that they could get a higher rate of pension under civilian legislation than they could under soldier legislation. They have asked me whether I thought they should drop the war veterans allowance and seek assistance under the Old Age Pensions Act. I have urged them not to do so. I told them that I was satisfied that this matter would be rectified. In the name of common justice it has to be rectified. Surely we are not going to place veterans in the position of getting a lower pension than a civilian pension. Can the minister tell us the number of applications for assistance under this fund and the number who were given assistance?

I have not before me the number of applications for assistance. But in response to the other comment, I believe I did say that, by and large, an attempt was being made to have some relationship between the war veterans allowance and the old age pension in conjunction with the provinces. Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba-we will leave out Saskatchewan, because I am not sure-there is
[Mr. Pearkes.l
not a veteran in any of these provinces who, when he reaches the age of seventy, will want to switch over to old age pension. I think that is a fair average. If the other two or three provinces have a slight edge after the age of seventy, then it must be kept in mind that the others have not.

This is the item having to do with the war veterans allowance board. The minister has not given an answer to the question asked this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver East respecting the husband and wife, where the wife had been working during some of the war years. The hon. member said that the war veterans allowance had been cut right off, and that the department was trying to collect even the man's small pension.
If that is so, then surely something should be done about it. There was probably no intention of misrepresentation at all in that instance. I do not believe it is fair to cut war veterans allowance off completely. I can quite understand why there would be some collection, or why something should be taken from the war veterans allowance. But these people have to live. They certainly cannot get city relief, and they cannot work.
I am surprised that the war veterans allowance board would take away the complete allowance. In cases I have had, where there have been overpayments, they have deducted $5 or $10 a month, or some such figure, leaving something on which the people could live. But in the case mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member the whole allowance was taken away.

I thought it would be impossible in committee to assess all the factors affecting an individual case, without having the record before us. I told the hon. member for Vancouver East that I would be glad to discuss the matter fully with him, and look into it.
Is it the practice of the board in such cases to cut off war veterans allowance completely?
There has not come to my attention any case similar to the one mentioned this afternoon.
I am quite satisfied that that is what has been done in this instance. I am sure there is not the slightest doubt about it at all.

Item agreed to.
534.	Veterans' insurance, $80,705.

Would the minister tell us how successful the veterans insurance scheme has been? I notice there is a decrease of

$17,624 from last year. Has the amount of insurance in force dropped? In other words, are there a number of people who have entered the scheme and ceased to pay premiums, so that the amount in force is smaller than it was before? I notice on looking at the details at page 308 that there are only two permanent employees in the department with total salaries of $4,470, whereas the salaries of temporary employees come to $66,015. What is the reason for that? Are there only two permanent employees because it is anticipated that the veterans insurance scheme will peter out? What is the story behind it?

As to the decrease of $17,624 from last year, this item covers administration and, as the hon. member will realize, in the first few years after demobilization there was a rush for applications. That rush is now tapering off, and consequently some saving has been made. It does not indicate at all, however, that the scheme is unsuccessful.
Something similar could be said with respect to permanent and temporary employees. I regret exceedingly to report what appears in the main estimates, namely the small proportion of permanent employees in my department. The deputy minister assures me there are some we have had before us that are going through now.
This department of course, in the long range of history, is considered a temporary department. If we have no more wars, then some day it will be merged with something else. Even so, however, the number of permanent employees is no reflection upon the permanency of the project. If the hon. member is interested, I could give him some figures. There are 23,025 policies in force under the plan, representing a capital of $65,851,985 insurance.
There is a very restricted list of people who may be named as beneficiaries under soldiers' insurance. Would the minister give the committee that list?
The list of beneficiaries includes the wife, or mother, or father, or children, or blood relations. That seems to be fairly wide.

A number of cases have been brought to my attention where soldiers have wished to leave the residue of their insurance to people other than those in the restricted list, and for very good reasons. In some cases the relatives were quite able to take care of themselves, and were not in this country. There might be some who are not direct blood relations to whom a person might wish to leave his estate or his insurance.
The information given me by the department is that under the law at the present
Supply-Veterans Affairs time a soldier cannot leave insurance to his estate; he must leave it to some direct relative, if such a relative is living. The only way that can be overcome is through an order in council passed by the cabinet. It seems to me there should be some easier way of doing it than by having to pass a special order in council concerning each individual case. Are those beneficiaries named in the act, or is it a regulation? If it is a regulation, it can be changed. If they are actually named under the act, then perhaps the act should be amended, because in some cases it is causing a lot of trouble.

The beneficiaries are named under the act. I think there is a certain amount of reason for the limitation, because the taxpayers pay the administration costs for this insurance. It was never intended that veterans insurance should compete with private insurance in any way. It was intended for men and women who might not, because of their service, be able to pass the medical examinations necessary to obtain ordinary insurance. It was in order to assist them to get insurance to take care of their dependents after they died. There was no intention whatever of having other Canadians pay the administration cost and provide the means whereby these veterans could build up an estate to be put to some impersonal use after their death.

The minister says that this insurance is costing the taxpayers money. Can he give us figures to prove that veterans insurance is being paid for out of taxpayers' money? Have the premiums that have been paid up to date not been pretty well sufficient to meet the cost of the insurance plan? Has he any figures that will indicate to the committee what it is costing the taxpayers?

I cannot tell you what it has cost since the beginning, but it is costing this year a total of $98,329, and we estimate that it will be $80,000 next year. It has been much more than that in past years. It has been worked out actuarially so that, with the administration costs being taken care of by the taxpayers, the capital amount of the insurance will take care of payments to beneficiaries in cases of death; but it is completely non-profit as far as that is concerned.

The minister said there were 23,025 policies in effect at the present time. What was the number a year ago? What I am trying to get at is whether the number of policies has increased during the past year or whether quite a number of men took out these policies and then forfeited them.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
The figure I gave was for August this year. The number in force as of August last year was 20,522 policies, and the total value was $58,627,691.
The experience is that the number of policies and the amount are going up.
Yes, steadily going up.
That is satisfactory.

While I am on my feet, perhaps I can answer a question that was asked about the assistance fund of the War Veterans Allowance Act. The total amount expended to date is $44,773.14, and the amount committed is $140,000.
In addition?
No, including.
Have any of these veterans' policies lapsed up to the present time? If so, how many?
Up to August 31, 1949, 616 policies had lapsed, of a total value of $2,199,000.
Is that because the veterans were not able to continue paying the premiums or did they lose interest in the insurance?
It is very difficult to say.

Item agreed to.
Payments to or for veterans and dependents-
535.	Pensions for disability and death, including pensions granted under the authority of the civilian government employees (war) compensation order P.C. 45/8848 of 22nd November, 1944, which shall be subject to the Pension Act, $100,664,000.
In respect to disability pensions I should like to ask the minister how many veterans have had their pensions reduced since January 1, 1949, and how many have been reduced by 25 per cent or more.

I have not those figures. I will ask the chairman of the pension commission to get them for me for next week. In the case of world war I, as the hon. member knows, those in force for three years or more are not reduced.

When the special committee on veterans affairs sat in 1946 the chairman of the pension commission tabled a statement showing among other things the number of disability decisions which had been rendered by the Canadian pension commission in respect to the second world war. According to that statement, unfavourable decisions- in other words, entitlement was not granted -amounted to 7,810 in the case of men who had served overseas; entitlement was refused

on the ground that the condition was of preenlistment origin and not aggravated on service. The figure for those who served only in Canada was 54,207. In other words, at that time there was a total of over 61,000 applications that had been refused although the men were disabled. Those applications were refused on the ground that they were suffering from pre-enlistment conditions, not aggravated on service.
Subsequently I obtained the figures for the period up to the 30th of June, 1947. At that time the figure was 13,321 for men who had actually gone overseas and, mind you, they had been discharged as disabled but were ruled out on application for pension on the ground that they had pre-enlistment conditions. The figure for men who served in Canada only was 72,340 as of June 30, 1947. Can the minister give us the figures for the period from the 30th of June, 1947, to the 30th of June, 1949? If he has any difficulty in tracing this matter he will find the discussion in 1947 Hansard at page 5777.
The chairman of the pension commission tells me he will be glad to furnish that information for next week.
When a pensioner has been re-boarded is there any court of appeal or tribunal to which he can appeal if he feels he has been aggrieved by the finding of the board?
Briefly, the answer is yes; he can ask for an appeal.
That is subject to new evidence being produced.
Subject to any new evidence being brought in.

I am not sure whether the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra asked this question, because I could not quite hear him. Can the minister say how many cases were reviewed as a result of the amendment that was made striking out the words "wilfully concealed", and how many pensions were increased as a result of that review?
Every case has been reviewed or is under review; and we shall be glad to provide the figures requested.
With respect to the matter I mentioned in my last question, I should like to ask the minister whether that appeal is handled by the same board that considered the case in the first place.

Since this matter has been brought up in other cases, rather than just give a snap reply to that question I should like to give a more complete statement, after consultation with the chairman of the board,

on the procedure followed in reviewing cases. I shall do that before the estimates are finished.

I have often wondered to what extent the report of the doctor who examines a young man at the time of enlistment is taken into account when it later becomes a question of determining whether or not that man is entitled to a pension. I am thinking of case after case which have come to my notice in which a man, upon applying for a pension due to disability, has been told that he is suffering from a pre-enlistment complaint. But this pre-enlistment complaint, if that is the correct term, is only discovered after the man has put in his service and applies for a pension. Apparently the report of the examining doctor which certified the man to be in A-l condition does not count for much. For instance, the doctor reports that the man is capable of taking his place in air crew, which I take it means that he is in A-l condition. After service of perhaps six months or a year, either in Canada or abroad, he is stricken with a heart condition, and it is suddenly discovered that he had a pre-enlistment condition, rheumatic fever or something of the kind, which produced that heart weakness.
It must be awkward for the department to discover that the army doctor passed as fit a man who, within a year or two, turned out to be not fit. The fact is, however, that he was certified as fit, was taken into the army or air force and put through those severe ^physical tests which young men have to undergo nowadays in their training. There are so many of these cases in which, after a year or two, men are found to be suffering from pre-enlistment ailments. That must be an awkward situation to handle. Apparently the report of the doctor who made the first examination is not given a great deal of weight, while on the other hand the report of the doctor who discovered the pre-enlistment disability seems to carry great weight with the department.
Perhaps the minister would comment on that situation. I hope I have not been bitter about it; I do not mean to be, but these boys can be pretty bitter. I have in mind the case of a young man who enlisted in the air force and was pronounced A-l. He joined the air crew, and a little later the very thing I have been mentioning happened to him; a year or so later he was found to have a heart condition. He was granted one-fifth total disability pension. If I were a lawyer I would argue that the mere fact that D.V.A. granted him anything at all was proof that the department thought he was entitled to something, and that his application was 45781-41
Supply-Veterans Affairs sound in that his ailment had been at least aggravated by his service. This boy is absolutely unable to do anything. When he shakes your hand his hand is soft and warm, and he has difficulty in walking for even a few steps. He appealed to the pension board and was granted another one-fifth, which again would indicate that the department recognized that he had some claim. He now receives a two-fifths disability pension, but the lad is absolutely unable to work. The doctors say they discovered that he had an attack of rheumatic fever early in life, and no doubt his heart condition resulted from that. I do not dispute that; I am not a doctor. However, this is one of those unfortunate cases where the department may be right, but what are you going to do with this boy? That is the point. You cannot blame these fellows for getting bitter. They joined up in all good faith. They were rated A-l, and went to work.
I should like the minister to comment on that situation, because there must be hundreds of similar cases. To repeat my main point, here is a doctor who certifies a man as A-l, or whatever the term may be, and he is sent to fight. Then some time later the department comes along and says the first doctor was wrong, that the man had a preenlistment ailment. They say doctors differ and patients die. In this case the boy is not dead yet, but I should like to know which doctor was right.

My hon. friend has opened up a topic which has run through the discussion of veterans affairs for many years. My first thought was that the best I could do would be to send him extracts from the proceedings of the last parliamentary committee, where the matter was discussed at great length, to show that one more attempt was made to do something about this matter. I know the pension board is attempting to interpret this legislation to the very best of its judgment. As my hon. friend said, the board has a tremendously difficult problem, but it is trying to administer the act fairly. When there is a pre-enlistment condition which in the opinion of the board has worsened owing to war service, pension is awarded to the extent of the service aggravation. I do not want to go into the question of what the doctors were doing when they examined the men on enlistment. As my hon. friend knows very well, many men went into the service who the doctors and everyone else knew were not one hundred per cent perfect specimens, whatever the documents may have shown.

I was rather struck by this item because it shows an estimated reduction for this year of $8,810,000, and I did not

Supply-Veterans Affairs expect to see a reduction of that amount, particularly in this item. Turning to the details on page 308 we find a reduction of over 25 per cent in the pensions paid to veterans of the northwest rebellion of 1885. This is to be expected, because these are all old men and naturally they are dying off rapidly. Then there is a reduction of some $4 million in connection with world war I, which is also to be expected. But when we come to world war II we also find a reduction of over $4 million. When we were considering the matter of pensions in the veterans affairs committee many very interesting figures were given to us purporting to show that the cost of veterans services, particularly pensions, as far as world war II veterans were concerned, would increase for some years to come. As I remember it, a constant increase was expected in the number of pensioners for world war II. Apparently for this particular year a considerable reduction is estimated. Would the minister comment on that and explain why that reduction is taking place? Has the department now come to the conclusion that the other proposition was wrong and the cost of pensions for world war II will not be increasing, as I believe actually happened in so far as world war I was concerned?
If I understood the minister correctly, the increase in pension which was retroactive is responsible for more than $4 million of this $58 million shown in 1948-49.
Oh, yes.
That is the situation then.

Yes, one could work it out, although I have not the figure here. I believe between seven and eight million dollars would be chargeable to the year before; but since it was voted last year, it is shown in these estimates in that column.

Then, I take it this information we received in the veterans affairs committee, that the cost of pensions for world war II would continue to increase for several

years, is correct. I should like to ask the minister what the general rate of that increase is expected to be percentagewise?

Perhaps if I gave the hon. member the number of pensions in force for the last five years, it would give a better indication than an estimate as to what might happen in the future. Going back to 1944-45, the number of pensions in force for world war II was 26,924; 1945-46, 53,293; 1946-47, 88,233; 1947-48, 103,963; 1948-49, 108,531.

I would be inclined to think that only the last year or two would give any indication of the rate of increase, since the earlier years given were those immediately following the war when there would not be a large number of people making application for pensions. May I ask how long it is estimated the amounts required for pensions for world war I will continue to increase?
Mr. Chairman, the amount for world war I is decreasing slightly now and will continue to decrease at a slightly increasing rate from year to year, one would expect, owing to mortality.
What about world war II?
World war II pensions will continue to increase for the next few years at any rate.
Is there any estimate as to how long that will continue?
Nothing but a guess.

Mr. Chairman, on the pension item I have a case which I think should be investigated by the department. It concerns the widow of an air force man who was sent by the air force to fly with one of those private companies-in this case Dominion Skyways. He was sent over to do a job with this company which was carrying on training. In the course of that work he was killed. Apparently the pilots who were doing this particular work were covered by an insurance policy which would return the same amount to the widow as she would have received if her husband had been killed in the air force.
When the husband lost his life, the widow was asked to make an application in accordance with the rules and regulations under which the ordinary veteran's widow would get a pension. This woman received the Cross of Sacrifice and her case was treated in exactly the same way as if the husband had been shot down overseas. Everything was all right until the pension increase was granted a year or two ago. This widow now finds that she does not get any increase whereas the widow of an airman who was killed overseas does receive that increase.

I do not suppose there would be more than a handful of these cases, but I do suggest some provision should be made to give those widows the increase. It might have to be done by order in council in each case. I do not know how that situation could be met, but certainly there is an unfairness which should be rectified.

In addition to the one case mentioned, Mr. Chairman, there are several others. Discussions are now under way between my department and the Department of National Defence with a view to seeing what can be done.

One other question. In my remarks this afternoon I referred to the case of the merchant navy lad who is suffering from tuberculosis. The disease was incurred during his service and it might have been cured had the manning pool doctor not sent him back to work instead of following the recommendation of the doctor who took the X-ray to give him six months' rest. Is there not some way in which a case of that type could be covered by our legislation? If not, the legislation is certainly defective.
I cannot answer that offhand, but I shall look into it.

Item agreed to.

536.	War veterans allowances, $19,825,000.

On item 536, I should like to ask the minister whether or not a person without any additional income, and who falls within the requirements of the act, could make application for assistance from this special fund in a case of hardship arising from unusual circumstances? For example, if a man's home burned down, could he make application for assistance?
Yes, Mr. Chairman. It was hoped the fund would be useful to cover situations such as that.
Was the minister going to give us the number of applications for assistance under this item and the number of applications granted?
Mr. Chairman, I gave the total amount a short time ago. I have not the figures here tonight for the number of applications, but I shall get them.

538. Unemployment assistance, $75,000.

Is that the old provision under which relief was given to small pensioners?
Supply-Veterans Affairs
Yes.
In other words, this is really much the same thing as the previous item which is made up of $500,000 for war veterans allowance recipients.
Pensioners of world war I. This item has a much longer history than has the other item.

Item agreed to.
Payments to or for veterans and dependents-
539. Hospital and other allowances, $4,310,000.

It is quite conceivable that the matter to which I should like to refer does not come under this item; but it is also quite conceivable that it might not come under any particular item. If I am out of order, possibly I could be told where I could more properly deal with the matter I have in mind. While on a western tour last spring the Prime Minister, according to press reports, visited the ex-servicemen who were in Colonel Belcher hospital. In the course of his visit among the men he met one from my constituency, a veteran of world war I who has been hospitalized now for a period of from two to three years. This veteran spends his spare time making articles such as purses out of leather. He asked the Prime Minister if he thought it fair that he should have to pay the sales tax on these commodities, most of which are given away. According to the press report, the Prime Minister said that certainly his request for relief from the payment of that tax seemed reasonable, and that he would make representations to the Minister of Finance. There must be a great many cases of that character in the various military hospitals across Canada. The fact that these men are able to do that type of work naturally assists them materially. I would say that it assisted them mentally in as great a way as any. It is quite possible that the minister cannot say whether or not the Prime Minister made the representations to the Minister of Finance; but may I ask the Minister of Veterans Affairs if he will make such representations, because then I shall be in a much better position to ask the Minister of Finance when we are dealing with matters relating to the Department of Finance.

Without having any knowledge of the incident referred to, I can say that the matter mentioned by the hon. member for Red Deer has come to our attention in other connections. I can assure him that, as in the past, every effort will be made to do this if

Supply-Veterans Affairs it is possible. It is not perhaps as great a hardship as appears on the surface, because a great deal of assistance is given to the patients in hospitals in this work which is done partly for the improvement of their disability and in some cases for their amusement and entertainment, in conjunction with the work of the Red Cross; and I think a patient is rarely charged an amount that he cannot easily bear. But I can assure my hon. friend that we will continue to look into the matter.

I would quite agree that probably there is not much money involved, but there is a principle involved. I think it would be a fine gesture on the part of the government if they could make this slight concession to these men. It is not so much a matter of the number of dollars involved as it is a matter of a vital principle.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Before we left the first item, the minister said that he preferred to deal with a number of the points that had been raised in the discussion on the first item, in relation to the specific items. One set of matters that was raised by hon. members over here had to do with the firefighters, the Red Cross nursing sisters and the auxiliary services generally. I have been looking down the list in order to try to see on what item we might ask the minister to deal with these people. The trouble is that they are not in under any item. Is this item not as good a one as any for the minister to comment on the appeals that have been made on behalf of members of the auxiliary services?

The items referred to would of course require legislation. In conformity with other departments, my department is not initiating legislation this session, except for purely administrative amendments to the Veterans Land Act to enable the experience gained in administering that act to bring about improvements in its flexibility and value to the veteran. But I do not propose to bring in at this session legislation covering the points referred to.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
May I ask whether that answer refers to one particular group, not excluding the importance of the others. Does that answer cover the case of the firefighters in all respects? One of the reasons I mention that group in particular is that, in the recommendations made by the veterans affairs committee at the end of their sittings in 1948, there were certain clear-cut recommendations with respect to the firefighters. I remember distinctly that one of the former members of the house, Mr. Eric McKay, the then member for Weyburn, gave notice of a motion to ask the house to approve that report. Word
IMr. Gregg.]
got around that such a motion might stand in the way of what its mover wanted, that there were some things in the report that the government could not accept, and that if that motion were pressed the government would be obliged to ask that it be voted down, and then we would lose everything in it. In the same way word got around to the effect that, if that motion were not pressed, maybe some things like the recommendation with respect to the firefighters would be implemented. I am not asking the minister to comment too much on what happened back in 1948, but I should like to know whether there is any further implementation of the committee's recommendation with respect to the firefighters and perchance other groups that could be carried out without this legislation that the minister says he is not going to introduce.
No. In my opinion, it could be carried out without legislation.

Item agreed to.
Miscellaneous payments-
542.	Last Post fund, $125,000.
I should like to ask several questions on this item. I can ask them all at once or one at a time, whichever the minister prefers.
One at a time.
My first question is this. How much is allowed per funeral? Is there a set price allowed or does it fluctuate according to the circumstances of the individual?
For the funeral $75 is allowed, plus the actual cost of the grave and the marker.
That is irrespective of the distance that might have to be travelled?
Yes. That is the maximum allowed.
A smaller amount might be allowed, though; is that not so?
Yes, if the maximum were not needed.

In other words, there is a sort of means test. I do not like to use the term "means test" now, although I think we should use it until it becomes so nauseating that i1 will be taken out of that legislation. But for want of a better term, is there some sort ol examination made of the circumstances and the amount given accordingly?
I am sorry; I did not get the Iasi question.
For instance, is it paid oui only to indigents or in cases of need?
Yes.

Is this a yearly appropriation which, if there is any balance left over, is carried over to another year? 1 notice the terminology used is, "Last Post fund". Is there a fund, and does it build up or fluctuate so that at the end of a year, if moneys are not spent, they revert to the treasury? If they do not revert to the treasury how much is in the fund now?

The unexpended portion reverts to the treasury each year so that the moneys for each year are revoted.
In a word, I should like to refer the committee to the excellent work done by private citizens across Canada who function without pay, without even their expenses being paid, as committees on behalf of the Last Post fund. I cannot speak too highly of them. There is a great deal more in looking after this matter in various sections of our country than appears on the surface. The committee which has functioned and is continuing to function under Mr. Norman Holland, which is national in scope with provincial and district subcommittees, is doing an excellent job. While this amount may appear small for each individual funeral, nevertheless there are activities and services given to the deceased veteran which do not appear in the dollar signs in these estimates.

I would join with the minister in these remarks and I would not criticize at all. In fact, I want to compliment the department on the work they are doing because occasionally, you know, I do have to bury people-and I should like to bury a lot more than I do, that is, politically.
I have found that there is a considerable appreciation among many people of the work done under this fund. I should like to ask one other question. It does not come under this item but I cannot help that, Mr. Chairman, because it does not come under any other item. In that I am like my friend the hon. member for Red Deer. There is a movement on foot, and I think all hon. members have received letters requesting that something should be done to assist the next of kin to visit the graves of their loved ones in war-stricken areas. I asked a question the other day in that respect, and I have forgotten who the appropriate minister was who answered it. The answer was that the government was not doing anything. I can quite understand that they cannot do anything at the moment. The answer also said that the Canadian Legion were thinking of some pilgrimage over to Europe for that purpose. Of course that does not fulfil the desires of many mothers, shall we say, who would like the
Supply-Veterans Affairs opportunity of visiting the graves of their sons, because mostly they just cannot afford to go there. I understand that this movement is gaining some momentum in the United States. I do not want any definite answer from the minister because I know that nothing is being done. We shall leave the question over. I suggest that the minister take that angle into consideration if it is at all possible. Perhaps there will be some development as time goes on.

Approximately twenty-five
years after the first great war there was a strong desire to revisit battlefields and the graves in Europe. Prior to 1936 the Canadian Legion, in co-operation with all the other veterans organizations, organized what became known as the Vimy pilgrimage. It was conducted entirely by the veterans organizations, and those who went on the pilgrimage themselves, by advanced planning, by working out the scheme with the so-called pilgrims, could pay their fees in advance into a central fund. Some six thousand went across the Atlantic in five ships and unveiled the Vimy memorial and visited the graves in France. That was a great undertaking. It was an undertaking that gave the greatest satisfaction to those who organized it and to those who took part in it. As I say, it was conducted entirely as an undertaking of the veterans organizations themselves and those who took part in it. Recently there have been indications of something of a similar interest. I have had a good many letters, as all hon. members have. The last world war was different. Instead of our casualties being concentrated in one general area they are all over the world. There are many of course without any known graves. I do not feel, at this particular time at any rate, that it is the role of my department to initiate any activities in that regard, particularly since the matter has again been discussed by the veterans organizations, and the president of one of them not so long ago made an announcement that they were attempting a study, as I answered the hon. member the other day, of piecemeal pilgrimages here and there, not on a wholesale scale as before, but in smaller bodies. I am quite sure that inquiries referred to the Legion would receive their attention, and in due course they might be able to do something about it.
As far as the United States is concerned, it has not yet passed any legislation on the matter. As a matter of fact the greater number of their dead have been or are to be moved, as I understand it, back for reburial in the United States.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
I should like to refer to a matter which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra brought up this afternoon and which quite properly comes under this item. We shall make some arrangements so that in the event of the funeral of a veteran under the Last Post fund, if he dies in hospital, the information will be made available. If it can be done in other deaths we shall attempt to let his old associates or his friends know about it.
Thank you very much.

Item agreed to.
543.	Grant to Canadian legion, $9,000.
Can the minister tell me how this grant is given out? Is it a single grant to the federal command, or is it distributed to the smaller branches?

Back about 1930 the department of that day, working in close co-operation on matters of service with the Canadian Legion, recognized that the service bureaux of that organization-the bureau here at dominion headquarters, and other service bureaux with paid secretariat throughout the provinces- were in reality, in the opinion of the department, doing useful work in connection with assembling information and evidence on pensions, and accepting a number of difficult tasks. It was arranged therefore at that time that the department would pay for assistance in maintaining such bureaux an amount of $10,000 in the beginning-and during the depression it went down to $9,000, with the understanding that the Canadian Legion would spend an equal amount for the service bureaux' work. Following it through in recent years they have spent more than three times as much as this amount each year in that work.

Item agreed to.
544.	Special grant to the Canadian legion toward the cost of the annual convention of the British Empire Service League to be held in Canada in September, 1949, $10,000.

Even though this item may pass automatically, I should like to say a word about it. Last spring it was indicated to the Prime Minister and myself that this year there was to be held in Ottawa the biennial conference of the British Empire Service League. It had been held only once before in Canada, and in the intervening years, up to the last war, had been held in London, Australia, and so on. As it was held at other capitals within the British commonwealth it had become the custom of governments of those countries to act to some degree as host to the delegates coming from all parts of the empire and commonwealth.

This year, coming to Ottawa, most of them from soft-currency countries, it was considered that this amount should be placed in the estimates to assist in travelling expenses within Canada, and in entertainment here. I am sure those hon. members who saw them lined up in the balcony, representing some twenty-three different countries of the commonwealth, must have felt that it was a rather important occasion, and perhaps worthy of this expenditure.
